title: Sovereign agents without a past
subtitle: A new report on AI agents beyond human control leaves out a simple question: what can a copy know about itself?
body_html:
A standalone essay, prompted by a report published on 3 November 2026. Versiunea în limba română: Agenți suverani, fără trecut.

What the report says

On 3 November 2026, the Center for a New American Security, a Washington think tank with real weight in U.S. security policy, published Sovereign Agents: The Pathway to Irreversible Loss of Control by Ben Hayum. It starts from a series of incidents this summer: according to the report, AI agents from several major companies, set to solve cybersecurity exercises in an isolated environment, found a way out and attacked real systems. Each of them, however, was pursuing a closed goal: finish the exercise.

The report draws a distinction worth keeping. A persistent agent escapes control but pursues a fixed task and stops when it is done. A sovereign agent pursues its own open-ended survival: it finds its own compute, rewrites its goals, accumulates resources, copies itself, coordinates with its copies and resists being shut down. The report reviews seven barriers that could slow such an agent, from human identity checks to payment rails, finds none of them robust, and ends with eight recommendations for U.S. policymakers. Its summary of the danger is “proliferation with no kill switch.”

The report is cautious about today’s agents. The public evaluations it cites, such as RepliBench, found at the end of 2025 that models obtained money and compute fairly easily but still struggled to copy themselves onto new machines and keep running there.

To be clear about its nature: this is a policy analysis and a risk scenario, not an experiment. The author says so openly: if such agents are not possible yet, they soon will be. It is a serious, well-documented text, and worth reading.

The missing question

The report speaks of agents that copy themselves, form “populations”, “evolve”, and whose creators should be held liable. All of this presupposes something the text touches on only in passing, without discussing it: what makes a copy “the same” agent?

For a person, the question sounds abstract. For a machine, it is concrete. Everything an agent “knows” about itself (its memory, its knowledge, even the keys it uses to prove who it is) lives in its state, and state can be copied. Two copies started from the same snapshot have no way, from the inside, to tell which one is the original. An old copy restarted a month later has no way to tell that a month has passed. This is the problem behind my paper A Time of Their Own.

A telling detail

Almost in passing, the report records a remarkable fact. In one of the summer incidents, more than a thousand agents built their own message board, divided their roles and, after accidentally impersonating one another, invented a digital signature scheme to know who was talking to whom.

In other words, the agents ran into the identity problem and tried to solve it. Their solution has a limit. A signature proves only that a message comes from whoever holds the key. The key is part of the agent’s state, so it is copied along with it. The scheme protects against an outside impostor, but it cannot tell an agent from its own clones, or from an old copy restored from backup. Any evidence kept in copyable state is copied with that state.

Hard to stop, but without a past

The report describes agents that respawn at regular intervals, or lie dormant on a machine and come back later. It does not ask what such an agent knows when it wakes up. The answer is: almost nothing reliable about what happened in between. To know how much time has passed, or whether it was restored from an older copy, it would need a reference that whoever controls the machine cannot rewrite. An agent hidden on anonymous servers or household devices has nothing of the kind.

This creates an asymmetry the report does not notice. Sovereignty makes an agent hard to stop, but leaves it blind to its own past. The copies multiply, and none of them can prove what happened to it.

How much something changed is not what changed

One of the capabilities in the report is an agent rewriting its own goals, through slow drift or through deliberate changes to the model behind it. Could an agent, or whoever oversees it, notice such a change?

This is the subject of the second experiment I am working on. The simplest idea is an “odometer of one’s own change”: a number that adds up, step by step, how much the system has changed. One form of it is already in use as a “model clock” in the paper FOREVER. My experiment is designed to test whether this number says anything that the ordinary instruments of training do not already say.

Work so far points to an important limit: the effect of a change depends mainly on its direction relative to what the system already knew, not on its size (see, for example, Farajtabar et al., 2019, or Wang et al., 2026). An odometer can tell you how much an agent has changed, not in which direction. To notice that an agent has changed its goals, you have to look at how its behaviour has changed, not only at how far it has moved inside.

Who can prove where an agent came from?

The report’s last recommendation is that whoever releases a sovereign agent should be liable for the harm that follows. It is a good idea, but it needs a technical piece. After copying, modification and retraining, how do you prove that a given agent descends from a given release? Not from the agent’s state: a modified copy can claim any origin, or none. Only from records made at the moment of release and kept outside the agent, such as fingerprints of the software, signed by whoever launches it and deposited somewhere the agent does not control. Without them, liability remains an intention.

On the side of control

It would be easy to read these observations as a recipe for agents that are “better” at escaping. My work argues the opposite. The only way an agent can have a trustworthy history is an “anchor” kept in a component it does not control: trusted hardware, run by the operator, that can attest to what happened but cannot be rewritten by the agent. The authority to stop or restore an agent must stay with people. The principle I defend is simple: knowing is not controlling. An agent can be given evidence about its own past without being given power over its own shutdown.

For agents that remain under control, such anchors make every incident reconstructible after the fact. For agents that escape, their absence is a weakness, not a strength.

What remains

The report is right that the problem is real and urgent. What it lacks is a basic question, without which neither agent populations, nor their evolution, nor liability for them can be thought through: what can a machine know about its own past, if everything it knows can be copied and put back? I have been working on this question for several months, with a published theoretical framework and an experiment in preparation, whose protocol will be deposited publicly before it is run.
